## Previously ...

Twenty-two lectures of individual metrics: reach, conversion rate, CAC, LTV,
ROAS, contribution, attribution, lift.

. . .

A board does not want a list of metrics. It wants a **structure**, and it
increasingly wants one that does not stop at money.

<!-- Speaker notes: this lecture carries LO6 and LO8 and is the merge of two
     earlier sessions. If time is short, cut section 3 (successors) rather than
     section 4, which is LO6's only home. -->

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Describe the Balanced Scorecard and its marketing application
- Compare it to later frameworks and select one for a given organisation
- Explain why marketing performance measurement now includes non-financial metrics
- Evaluate a sustainability claim against its evidence

# 1. Why a Framework

## The Metric Sprawl Problem

A GA4 property exposes several hundred metrics. Your dashboard could show any of
them.

. . .

Without a structure, three things happen, reliably:

- The report becomes a **data dump**, and nobody reads past the first screen
- The client picks the **flattering number**, because you offered it
- Nobody can say whether the quarter was good, because there is no agreed answer
  to what good means

. . .

**A framework is a commitment made in advance about which numbers count.** It is
the pre-registration habit from Lecture 8, at organisational scale.

## What a Framework Actually Does

1. **Selects.** A small set of metrics, chosen before the results are in
2. **Structures.** A hierarchy, so a number has a parent it explains
3. **Connects.** Every metric attaches to a stated objective
4. **Forces trade-offs into the open.** Two metrics that pull against each other
   are visible on the same page rather than argued about separately

. . .

The fourth is the one that makes frameworks uncomfortable, and the reason they
are worth having.

# 2. The Balanced Scorecard

## Kaplan and Norton, 1992

Robert Kaplan and David Norton's argument was simple and, at the time, radical:

> Financial measures are **lagging** indicators. They tell you the result of
> decisions taken quarters ago, and they tell you nothing about whether the next
> quarter will be any good.

. . .

Managing on financial measures alone therefore encourages exactly the behaviour
that produces good numbers now and a weaker business later: cutting training,
deferring maintenance, under-investing in the customer relationship.

. . .

**Their fix was to make three other kinds of measure equally visible.**

## The Four Perspectives {.smaller}

| Perspective | The question | A marketing metric |
|---|---|---|
| **Financial** | How do we look to shareholders? | Contribution, ROAS, CAC payback |
| **Customer** | How do customers see us? | NPS, retention, share of wallet |
| **Internal process** | What must we excel at? | Campaign cycle time, lead response time |
| **Learning and growth** | Can we keep improving? | Test velocity, skills, data quality |

. . .

Note where this module's own subject sits. **Data quality is a learning and
growth metric**, which is why the cleaning log in Lecture 17 is a management
artefact and not just good manners.

## Strategy Maps

The perspectives are not a list. They are a **causal chain**, read from the
bottom up:

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-align: center
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  L["<b>Learning &amp; growth</b><br>analyst skills,<br>data quality"] --> P["<b>Internal process</b><br>faster tests,<br>quicker response"]
  P --> C["<b>Customer</b><br>better experience,<br>higher retention"]
  C --> F["<b>Financial</b><br>contribution,<br>growth"]
```

. . .

**Drawing the map is the exercise that exposes the assumptions.** Every arrow is
a claim that one thing causes another, and most organisations have never tested
any of them.

## Criticisms Worth Taking Seriously

- **Static.** Built annually, in a world that moves quarterly
- **Top-down.** Cascaded from the board, so the people measured did not choose
  the measures
- **Slow.** Some measures cannot be updated more often than they can be collected
- **Causality is assumed, not demonstrated.** The arrows on the strategy map are
  hypotheses, and they are rarely tested even when the data exists

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The last one is the interesting criticism for this module. You spent Lecture 21
learning how to test a causal claim. Almost nobody applies it to their own
strategy map.
:::

# 3. Successors

## OKRs {.smaller}

**Objectives and Key Results**: one qualitative objective, three to five
quantitative key results, reviewed quarterly.

> **Objective**: Become the obvious choice for Dublin deadstock buyers
>
> **KR1**: Repeat purchase rate from 18% to 26%
> **KR2**: Non-follower reach share from 41% to 55%
> **KR3**: Email list from 2,100 to 5,000

. . .

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

**Stronger than the scorecard at**

Cadence, focus, and getting the team to care

:::

::: {#second-column}

**Weaker at**

Trade-offs. Nothing in the format says what you are willing to lose

:::
::::

## The North Star Metric

One number the whole organisation is steered by, with a handful of input metrics
beneath it.

. . .

Attractive because it is simple, and **dangerous for exactly the same reason**.
Everything not in the number becomes invisible, and any single metric can be
moved in ways nobody intended.

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
If Loomrow's north star were "reach", the reel in Lecture 3 that reached 535,086
accounts and engaged almost none of them would be the best thing the company ever
did.
:::

## Marketing-Specific Scorecards

- **Funnel-stage scorecards**: a small set of metrics per stage, so awareness and
  conversion are not judged by the same number
- **Brand plus performance**: the long-term and short-term split, because the
  measurable half is the short-term half and budgets follow measurement
- **The Marketing Accountability Standards Board** line of work, on connecting
  marketing activity to financial outcomes in terms a CFO accepts

## Choosing One {.smaller}

| If the organisation is... | Consider |
|---|---|
| Small, fast, one marketing hire | OKRs. Quarterly, few metrics, low overhead |
| Large, board-governed, regulated | Balanced Scorecard, with a reporting calendar |
| Product-led with one clear behaviour | A north star, plus explicit guardrail metrics |
| Data-immature | Fewer metrics than you want, measured properly |

. . .

**The last row is the common case and the hardest advice to give**, because it
sounds like doing less. A framework the organisation cannot feed is worse than no
framework: it produces numbers nobody trusts and everybody quotes.

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

For Loomrow, or a company you know:

1. Build a four-perspective scorecard with two metrics per perspective
2. Draw the strategy map linking them
3. Mark every arrow that is **assumed** rather than measured
4. Say which framework you would actually recommend, and why

# 4. The Perspective Every Framework Now Needs

## Why This Is a Marketing Metrics Question {.smaller}

<!-- Speaker notes: regulation here moves fast and has been repeatedly amended,
     delayed and simplified. Check the current position of CSRD, the omnibus
     package and the Green Claims proposal before delivering this slide, and say
     plainly when something is in flux. -->

**Regulation.** EU corporate sustainability reporting obligations have been
extending non-financial disclosure well beyond the largest listed companies, and
separate work on substantiating environmental claims has been moving in parallel.
Both have been amended and delayed repeatedly, so **check the current position
before you rely on any of it**.

. . .

**Ireland specifically.** The Advertising Standards Authority for Ireland's code
covers environmental claims in advertising now, whatever happens at EU level.

. . .

**Stakeholders beyond shareholders.** Employees, customers, and above all
**procurement teams**: B2B buyers ask for this data in tenders, and an answer of
"we do not measure that" loses the tender.

## Reputational Risk Has a Price

Greenwashing is no longer a reputational abstraction. It is an advertising risk
with a measurable cost: campaigns withdrawn, rulings published, and the original
claim reprinted in every article about the ruling.

. . .

**The asymmetry is what matters for a marketer.** An unsupported green claim buys
a small lift in sentiment and risks a headline naming the brand. Most marketing
decisions do not have that shape.

## What Gets Measured: Environmental {.smaller}

The emissions of the marketing function itself, which are almost entirely
**Scope 3**:

- **Media delivery.** Every ad impression is computation plus transmission plus a
  device. Per-impression it is tiny; at campaign scale it is not
- **The ad tech supply chain.** A programmatic impression may pass through a
  dozen intermediaries, each with its own footprint
- **Production.** Shoots, travel, sets, samples
- **Events.** Usually the largest single line, and the easiest to count

. . .

Per-thousand-impression carbon estimates now exist and are increasingly requested
in media plans. **Treat the published figures as estimates with wide error bars**,
because that is what they are.

## Social and Governance {.smaller}

:::: {layout="[1,1]"}
::: {#first-column}

**Social**

- Representation in creative
- **Accessibility** of digital assets: alt text, captions, contrast, keyboard
  navigation
- Ad placement standards, and what your programmatic buying funds
- Supplier diversity

:::

::: {#second-column}

**Governance**

- Data protection compliance, as a reportable metric
- Consent rates and how consent is obtained
- Retention periods actually applied

:::
::::

. . .

**That governance column is Lecture 10, returning as a board metric.** The cookie
banner you wrote is now a number somebody reports.

## Measured, Estimated, or Asserted {.smaller}

The single most useful distinction in this whole area:

| | Example | What it supports |
|---|---|---|
| **Measured** | Event travel, from receipts | A claim, with a boundary |
| **Estimated** | Media delivery emissions, from a published model | A direction, with error bars |
| **Asserted** | "We are committed to sustainability" | Nothing |

. . .

Most published sustainability communication mixes all three **in the same
sentence**, and presents the whole thing at the confidence of the first.

## The Evidence Ladder {.smaller}

From the bottom:

1. **Sentiment.** "We care about the planet"
2. **Activity.** "We switched to recycled packaging"
3. **A number.** "We cut packaging emissions by 30%"
4. **A number with a boundary and a baseline.** "...across our own packaging,
   against 2023, excluding inbound freight"
5. **Audited**, by someone whose opinion is published
6. **Audited, and comparable**, against a standard others report to

. . .

**Marketing claims usually live on rungs 1 to 3. Procurement questions start at
rung 4.**

## Greenwashing Patterns {.smaller}

The recurring five. Once you can name them you will see them daily:

1. **Unbounded claims.** "Sustainable" with no scope. Sustainable compared to
   what, measured how?
2. **Shifted baselines.** Choosing the worst year as the starting point
3. **Offsets presented as reductions.** "Carbon neutral" where nothing was reduced
4. **Selective scope.** Reporting the 8% you control and omitting the 92% you buy
5. **Irrelevant precision.** "We saved 1,247,391 litres of water." Out of how
   much? Compared to what?

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The fifth is the one this module has already taught you to spot. Lecture 2's
spurious-precision slide was the same fault on a chart.
:::

## Putting Them on the Dashboard

Non-financial metrics get ignored when they are put somewhere ignorable: a second
tab, a footer, an appendix.

. . .

**Same page, same visual weight, or they will not be read.** That is a design
decision, and you learned how to make it in Lectures 6 and 7.

. . .

And apply the honesty rule from Lecture 17 here too: mark which figures are
measured, which are estimated, and which are somebody's assertion. A dashboard
that shows all three at the same weight is making the claim on rung 1 look like
rung 5.

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

Take a real brand's sustainability communication, on their own site:

1. List every quantitative claim it makes
2. For each, identify the **boundary**, the **baseline**, and whether it is
   audited
3. Rank the claims on the evidence ladder
4. Design two non-financial metrics you would add to that brand's marketing
   dashboard, and say where on the page they go

::: {#timer2 .timer seconds="1500"}
:::

# 5. AI, Frameworks and Claims

## AI This Block: A Producer

Where we are on the module's AI spine, set out in Lecture 1 and named properly in
Lecture 12:

> **A producer.** It drafts the spec, the report and the deck. You are still the
> one who signs it.

## Comparing Frameworks Is a Reading Task

This is well-documented territory, widely written about, and assistants handle it
well.

> "Compare the Balanced Scorecard and OKRs for a 12-person Irish e-commerce
> business with one marketing hire. Which fits, and why?"

. . .

Then the prompt that stops you accepting the first fluent answer:

> "Now argue for the one you rejected."

. . .

**It will argue that side just as fluently**, which tells you how much weight the
first answer deserved.

## The Greenwashing Machine

<!-- Speaker notes: strong exercise. Let them generate the fluent unfalsifiable
     claim themselves, then have to fix it. It lands far harder than an example
     from a slide. -->

Ask an assistant to write sustainability copy for a brand, and it will produce
exactly what section 4 warns about: unbounded, baseline-free, rung-one claims, in
confident marketing prose.

. . .

It is not being careless. **It is reproducing the genre**, and the genre is mostly
greenwashing.

## Using It the Other Way

Pointed at claims rather than producing them, it is a genuinely good auditor:

> "For each quantitative claim in this text, identify the boundary, the baseline,
> and whether it is verifiable. Flag anything unfalsifiable."

. . .

The same tool, the same afternoon, on both sides of the problem. **Which is the
clearest demonstration in this module that the tool is not the thing that has
judgement.**

## An AI-Drafted Claim Is Still Your Claim

There is no exemption for generated copy. Not in the ASAI code, not in
consumer-protection law, not in a tender response.

. . .

If a claim in your campaign turns out to be unsupported, "the assistant wrote it"
is the same defence as "the AI produced it" in Lecture 1, and it fails for the
same reason.

. . .

**Disclosure protects you. Delegation does not.**

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

1. Ask an assistant to write sustainability copy for a brand
2. Audit its own output with the prompt from two slides ago
3. Rewrite one claim so it would survive procurement scrutiny
4. Note what the rewrite cost you in punchiness, because that cost is the reason
   the original genre exists
